proposal.title: SEC Filing Reports Ramaswamy Held 8.4% of Strive
proposal.description_short: An SEC amendment reported Vivek Ramaswamy beneficially owned 5,693,897 Strive shares, or 8.4%, in a filing tied to an April 20, 2026 event.
proposal.description_medium: An SEC Schedule 13D amendment reported that Vivek Ramaswamy beneficially owned 5,693,897 shares of Strive, Inc., equal to 8.4% of the class on the filing’s stated conversion assumption. The filing identifies April 20, 2026 as the event date. It says the issuer’s at-the-market share sales ended the shareholder agreement and dissolved the reporting group; Ramaswamy continued to own more than 5%. The amendment does not support the held record’s 7.6% figure or May 28 date.
proposal.description_long: An SEC Schedule 13D amendment filed by Vivek Ramaswamy and other reporting persons states that he beneficially owned 5,693,897 Strive, Inc. shares, representing 8.4% of the class under the filing’s stated assumption that Class B shares convert to Class A. The filing identifies April 20, 2026 as the event date. It explains that Strive’s at-the-market share sales increased the number of outstanding shares, causing the reporting group to fall below the 50% voting-power threshold in its shareholder agreement. The agreement then terminated automatically, and the reporting persons ceased to constitute a group. The amendment says Ramaswamy still beneficially owned more than 5% and would report separately; the other exiting persons fell below 5%. This establishes an ownership disclosure and reporting change. It does not support the held entry’s claim of a 7.6% stake as of May 28, nor any assertion that his Ohio policy platform was designed to benefit Strive investors.

proposal.title: Birthright citizenship executive order and later court injunction
proposal.description_short: Birthright citizenship executive order and later court injunction
proposal.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the birthright citizenship executive order on January 20, 2025. It covered births where the mother was unlawfully present, or lawfully present temporarily, and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor lawful permanent resident; the order exempted children of lawful permanent residents. A Maryland judge issued a later nationwide injunction on August 7, Reuters reported.
proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies not to recognize U.S. citizenship for certain children born in the United States. The order covered births when the mother was unlawfully present, or lawfully present temporarily, and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor a lawful permanent resident; it expressly exempted children of lawful permanent residents. It was scheduled to apply to births more than 30 days after signing. The order’s signing and its later court challenges are separate milestones. Reuters reported that a Maryland federal judge issued a class-action injunction on August 7, 2025, the fourth nationwide injunction against the policy. The Supreme Court’s June 27 decision limited universal injunctions but did not decide whether this order complied with the Constitution. The cited records do not establish the held synopsis’s broad “neither parent” paraphrase, an annual estimate of 150,000 affected births, or an October 3 ruling date; those claims are omitted.

proposal.title: Justice Department announces zero-tolerance prosecution policy
proposal.description_short: The Justice Department announced a zero-tolerance prosecution policy for unlawful entry at the Southwest border.
proposal.description_medium: On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a zero-tolerance policy directing Southwest Border U.S. Attorney’s Offices to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals for unlawful-entry offenses, to the extent practicable. The release identified five districts and framed the policy as criminal enforcement; it did not expressly direct family separation.
proposal.description_long: On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a “zero-tolerance” policy for unlawful-entry offenses under 8 U.S.C. §1325(a). The Justice Department directed each U.S. Attorney’s Office along the Southwest Border to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals under that provision, to the extent practicable. The release described the policy as an escalated prosecution effort and listed the five affected districts: Southern California, Arizona, New Mexico, Western Texas and Southern Texas. It also referred to a prior April 2017 instruction prioritizing some immigration prosecutions. The Justice Department announcement establishes the prosecution policy and date. It does not say that the policy expressly directed family separation, state an intent to deter migration through separation, or establish the scale or duration of family separations. Those claims require separate reporting or records and should not be attributed to this announcement. The release ties the policy to prosecution of unlawful-entry referrals under 8 U.S.C. § 1325(a), subject to prosecutorial resources.
